extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, litigators, and clients involved in U.S. patent claim-construction (Markman) proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how Markman (claim construction) hearings in U.S. district courts are conducted and how to prepare/substantiate claim construction positions, including evidentiary preferences, timing, formats, and practical litigation support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Markman (Claim Construction) Hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markman hearing is a pre-trial hearing in a U.S. District Court during which a judge examines evidence from all parties on the appropriate meanings of relevant keywords used in a patent claim when patent infringement is alleged by a plaintiff. It is also known as a 'Claim Construction Hearing'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: determine meanings of claim terms so the court can establish the scope of asserted patent claims prior to infringement analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of Markman ruling
rubrics_metrics.description: The court determines patent infringement cases by interpreting the claims. A Markman hearing may encourage settlement since the judge’s claim construction finding can indicate a likely outcome of the patent infringement case as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: judge’s construction influences jury instructions and overall case strategy; early construction can narrow or resolve issues and prompt settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who decides claim meaning vs. infringement (judge vs. jury)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge will decide how the claims should be understood in his or her capacity as the legal arbiter. However, a jury decides whether or not there was infringement because they are the fact-finders. This includes situations where the doctrine of equivalents is being applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seventh Amendment context: while juries are fact-finders, claim construction is for the court; the judge’s construction will be reflected in jury instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic evidence is primary
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials provided as a part of the patent application are referred to as intrinsic evidence. This comprises the claims, executive summary, and written description contained in the patent application itself, written or verbal correspondence between the patent applicant and the patent examiner that includes the prosecution history, prior art cited in the patent application, and previous comparable patents and their prosecution histories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts generally look at intrinsic evidence to aid in claim construction; it is the starting point and often the decisive evidence for interpreting claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrinsic evidence is secondary/background
rubrics_metrics.description: Any evidence that originates from outside sources is considered extrinsic. Extrinsic evidence in Markman hearings may include: definitions from dictionaries for common terms, for technical words, consult encyclopedias or engineering dictionaries, journals, or other scholarly works that cover the technology, the patent applicant’s testimony, or expert opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrinsic evidence is helpful for education and background knowledge on the contested invention, even though courts generally look at intrinsic evidence to aid in claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phillips v. AWH Corp framework for claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: In Phillips v. AWH Corp, the Federal Circuit (2004) established the current method for construing patent claims. This case established a foundation for claim formation, as did later judgments that cited Phillips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The correct claim construction cannot be determined using a predetermined process; rather, a set of criteria are applied to choose the right construction. Courts apply Phillips' principles (focus on intrinsic evidence, appropriate role of extrinsic evidence, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO alignment with Phillips (37 CFR 42.100)
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Patent Office finalized a regulation to align its claim construction guidelines with the Federal Circuit’s Phillips ruling. The Patent Office will interpret patent claims for inter partes review (IPR), post-grant review (PGR), and covered business method patents (CBM) procedures in accordance with this rule, which is outlined in 37 CFR 42.100.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicability: this regulation applies to petitions submitted after it has been adopted; practitioners should note timing when preparing USPTO petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: District court discretion to hold a Markman hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: The district court has the discretion to determine whether a Markman hearing is required. A Markman hearing is not necessary as a result of the Markman v. Westview Instruments ruling; rather, patent claims are decided by a judge rather than a jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many district judges rule that a Markman hearing is not required; if paper records provide all relevant details, courts may resolve construction without a live hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formats of Markman hearings (paper-only vs live testimony)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markman hearing can be conducted in a variety of ways, but many lawyers and judges prefer the paper-only format to a multi-day live hearing with numerous witnesses. Some courts will permit specialists to testify without being questioned themselves or by outside witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider procedural strategy: paper-only submissions may be efficient; parties should plan for possible live testimony or technical tutorials depending on the court’s preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and procedural variability of Markman hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markman hearing is often scheduled at an advanced stage of the trial. Over time, several courts have created various procedures. Some districts reach early decisions on construction claims before talking about potential patent infringement. Other courts will hear all of the evidence, interpret the claim, and then give the jury instructions at the conclusion of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Litigators must check local practices and case schedule — timing affects strategy (e.g., early resolution vs. post-evidence construction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court must establish claim scope before analyzing the accused product
rubrics_metrics.description: Any patent litigation begins with the formulation of the patent claim. The court must establish the scope and significance of the asserted patent claims before looking at the allegedly infringing item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction defines what constitutes protected intellectual property and frames infringement and validity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of technical tutorials and visual aids to explain claimed subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: IIPRD provides experienced professionals to build and support claim construction theories and technical tutorials to help prepare charts that can assist in describing the claimed subject matter to the judges and present the facts in easy-to-understand ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-prepared tutorials and charts can clarify complex technical concepts for judges and support claim construction positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantiate claim construction via critical review of specification, prosecution history, and expert evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantiate claim construction through critical review of specification, prosecution history, and expert evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical step: systematically analyze intrinsic records and reconcile with expert testimony to support proposed constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare written opinions, notes, and documentation to support scope/interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft opinions, notes, and documentation required to substantiate the scope/interpretation of claims and/or claim terms/elements and limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparation of clear written positions (claim construction briefs, rebuttals, exhibits) is essential to persuade the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish credibility and credentials of the testifying expert
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish credibility and credentials of the testifying expert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert qualification and credibility are crucial when extrinsic evidence or expert opinion is relied upon; prepare CVs, prior publications, and direct testimony to build reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop validity defenses with comprehensive claim charts mapped to prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up a validity defence through comprehensive claim charts demonstrating scope of each claim term/element/limitation and mapping with prior art reference(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use detailed claim charts to show how prior art reads on claim elements and to support invalidity arguments or to refine claim meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare claim construction contentions in compliance with USPTO/claim construction guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: IIPRD supports clients with preparation of patent claim construction contentions in compliance with claim construction guidelines established by the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure petitions and contentions (in court or at the PTO) conform to applicable guidance (e.g., Phillips principles, 37 CFR 42.100) and procedural rules to avoid waiver or rejection.
